lines.text: Was this written by an AI? There is a way to tell, and it's hiding in the words.

lines.source: Sec. 1.2 (many plausible next tokens when entropy is high)
lines.text: When an AI writes, every next word is a choice. Usually, many words would fit.

lines.source: Sec. 3, Alg. 2 (hash of the previous token seeds the green list)
lines.text: So before each word, a simple rule splits the whole vocabulary in two: a green list and a red list.

lines.source: Sec. 3 (soft watermark: green tokens promoted, not forced)
lines.text: The lists reshuffle with every word, and the AI is gently nudged to pick from green.

lines.source: abstract (negligible impact on text quality, invisible to humans)
lines.text: The text reads just as well. Without the rule, there is nothing to see.

lines.source: Sec. 2 (a human is expected to hit green with half of their tokens)
lines.text: Now check it. A person has no idea which words are green, so they land on green about half the time, like tossing a coin.

lines.source: Sec. 2 (one-proportion z-test on the green count)
lines.text: The AI's text lands on green again and again. A few sentences in, that's a coin coming up heads far too often to be luck.

lines.source: Sec. 2 (detection does not require access to the model)
lines.text: And checking needs only the rule, not the AI that wrote it.

lines.source: Sec. 7 (attacks: about a quarter of the tokens or more must change)
lines.text: It isn't magic. Rewrite a large part of the text and the pattern fades. And it's only there if the AI's maker switches it on.

lines.source: Ural and Yoshigoe, IEEE Access 2024 and 2025
lines.text: Text is one thing an AI makes. The model itself is another, and models get copied. That's the part I work on: a signature trained into the model, so its owner can prove it's theirs.
More and more of what we read and run is made by machines. Knowing where it came from is becoming a basic need.
